title: Shipment exceptions, handled before the customer calls
subtitle: From three conflicting requests to rules that run as tests, a working control tower and a controlled pilot — for a fictional short-sea and door-to-door operator.
disclosure: Independent portfolio case. Tidewell Logistics is fictional. Workshops, sprints and acceptance testing are simulated; figures are illustrative assumptions. The automated tests and the demo are real; nothing was deployed in a real organisation.
role: Business analyst in a Scrum team: problem framing, discovery and workshops, process and rule design, backlog preparation with the Product Owner, UX, acceptance and production readiness.

executed.label: Executed
executed.meaning: Run by a tool in this repository — tests in CI, the working demo

validated.label: Validated model
validated.meaning: Standard file checked by a validator (BPMN 2.0, DMN 1.3, OpenAPI 3.1)

documented.label: Documented analysis
documented.meaning: Analysis or design written for the fictional organisation

proposed.label: Proposed design
proposed.meaning: Target design or plan; not built or run in a real organisation

simulated.label: Simulated
simulated.meaning: Fictional workshops, interviews, sprints, BAT or pilot readouts — shows format and decisions

pending.label: Pending real validation
pending.meaning: Needs real people, real data or a real system

pillars.title: Problem before solution
pillars.text: Three requested solutions reframed as one missing set of rules.

pillars.title: Rules that run as tests
pillars.text: 13 rules, a DMN table and 30 examples executed in CI.

pillars.title: A working control tower
pillars.text: The release, built on the same rules, with a guided scenario.

pillars.title: Controlled pilot
pillars.text: BAT, go/no-go, rollback and a stage gate before scaling.

challenge.title: Customers hear it at the gate
challenge.text: Only 22% of late deliveries were announced before the window started.

challenge.title: Customer service as a switchboard
challenge.text: ±1,250 “where is my load?” contacts a week — 38% of all contacts.

challenge.title: Nobody owns the exception
challenge.text: Planners notice delays by chance and copy orders into Excel.

myRole.title: Analysis
myRole.text: Problem framing, options and business case, discovery, event storming, registers.

myRole.title: Process and rule design
myRole.text: BPMN 2.0 AS-IS/TO-BE, decision table and DMN, requirements with traceability.

myRole.title: Delivery and readiness
myRole.text: Backlog with the PO, UX, acceptance testing, go/no-go, support and measurement.

workstreams.title: Detect and classify
workstreams.tagline: Only what puts the promise at risk becomes an exception.
workstreams.problem: Every status change looked the same, so people filtered by gut feeling; three teams counted “late” differently.
workstreams.choice: Late = after the end of the agreed window (D-01). Severity from minutes late; reefer one level up; cancellations always critical.

workstreams.title: Own and resolve
workstreams.tagline: One list, one owner, one clock.
workstreams.problem: Delays were noticed by chance; nobody was accountable for acting within a time.
workstreams.choice: Owner group by cause; 30 min / 2 h response time as BPMN timer events; escalation to the shift lead; mandatory reason code.

workstreams.title: Tell the customer first
workstreams.tagline: One clear message, not a message storm.
workstreams.problem: Only key accounts whose account manager happened to know were told; standard TMS e-mails would be noise.
workstreams.choice: Notify major/critical, hold missing status until confirmed, throttle per order, recovery message only if told before, call key accounts.

workstreams.title: Prove it before scaling
workstreams.problem: The business case stands or falls with one unknown: how many “where is my load?” calls disappear.
workstreams.choice: Two-sprint pilot for five customers with a control group in shadow mode; fund release 2 only at ≥ 20% fewer WISMO contacts.

architecture.caption: Proposed: a small component next to the TMS (D-03). Implemented in the demo: the same rules and engine in the browser, on a mock API that follows the OpenAPI contract.

decisions.title: Late means after the window
decisions.text: Not after the planned ETA: most ETA changes do not affect the promise.

decisions.title: Severity decides who is told
decisions.text: Serves “never surprise a key account” and “no message storm” at once.

decisions.title: Build small, next to the TMS
decisions.text: Supplier date uncertain; rules stay portable if the supplier catches up.

decisions.title: Confirm missing status first
decisions.text: A false alarm costs more trust than a late one.

decisions.title: Pilot with a stage gate
decisions.text: Release 2 only if WISMO falls ≥ 20% against a control group.

decisions.title: Escalate, but keep the hold
decisions.text: Found by building the demo: overdue held exceptions go to the shift lead.

implementation.text: A planner sees the right exceptions
Key users incl. the sceptic; 6 findings

outcomes.label: Major/critical delays told before the window

evidence.title: Problem statement
evidence.why: Turns three requested solutions into one measurable problem with a root cause.

evidence.title: Options and business case
evidence.why: Four options on agreed weights; the riskiest assumption named and tested by a pilot.

evidence.title: Registers and strategic analysis
evidence.why: Assumptions, constraints, risks and dependencies with owners and triggers.

evidence.title: Stakeholders and RACI
evidence.why: Who decides what; the BA is responsible for much and accountable for little.

evidence.title: Event storming and facilitation
evidence.why: How two opposite positions became one concept (severity) and one decision owner.

evidence.title: Decision log
evidence.why: Options, owner, decision and consequence for every choice that shaped the release.

evidence.title: BPMN 2.0 AS-IS / TO-BE
evidence.why: Lanes per role, timer boundary events for response times; validated with bpmn-moddle.

evidence.title: Gap analysis and activity diagram
evidence.why: Each gap typed as system, policy, organisation or process — which decides the kind of work.

evidence.title: Exception rules and DMN 1.3
evidence.why: Decision tables in the OMG standard; a test proves they decide what the code decides (912 cases).

evidence.title: Executable acceptance examples
evidence.why: 30 Given/When/Then rows that run against the rule module in CI.

evidence.title: Requirements and traceability
evidence.why: Pain point → requirement → rule → story → test → KPI; IDs checked in CI.

evidence.title: Backlog, WSJF and release 2
evidence.why: Prioritised with the PO; a second iteration refined into slices with open questions.

evidence.title: UX specification and usability plan
evidence.why: Personas, flows, states, accessibility and eight UX decisions tied to user needs.

evidence.title: Logistics Control Tower
evidence.why: The release working end to end on the same rules; guided 10-step scenario.

evidence.title: Architecture and ADRs
evidence.why: Proposed vs. implemented; five decisions with alternatives and consequences.

evidence.title: OpenAPI 3.1 contract
evidence.why: Linted in CI; a contract test checks every response and example against it.

evidence.title: Test strategy and results
evidence.why: What actually ran — unit, contract, browser and accessibility tests — separate from simulated BAT.

evidence.title: BAT log and go/no-go
evidence.why: Key users, triage, sign-off with known issues, and the BA's own mistake (DEF-04).

evidence.title: Operations runbook and change plan
evidence.why: What support does when webhooks stop or messages go wrong; adoption and training per group.

evidence.title: Usability test with real people
evidence.why: Script, tasks and report template ready; the sessions themselves are not yet run.

limits: Fictional organisation; interviews, workshops, sprints, BAT and the pilot readout are simulated.
No real TMS, e-mail or load testing; the demo runs in the browser on a mock API.
Architecture, privacy and runbook are proposals, not reviewed by a real architect, DPO or support team.
No usability test with real participants yet.
lessons: Rules before screens: the gap was a missing definition, not a missing tool.
Passing stories are not a met need — three of four BAT majors came from real readers.
Building is a review: the demo exposed five open questions and a privacy leak.
Answer customer-facing questions with the PO, not alone (DEF-04).
